evaluation.positioning_hook: A burned-out school custodian in Pennsylvania races a 30-day screenplay deadline while juggling two jobs, a strained daughter, and a second chance at the life he gave up.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The emotional promise is clear and accessible: a working-class father trying to reclaim a buried creative life. The audience is real but narrower than a high-concept commercial feature, and the hook depends on character empathy more than plot fireworks.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands early and cleanly: Ralph is a custodian with a screenplay contest deadline and a life that keeps interrupting the dream. The hook is easy to explain, though it plays more as a strong dramatic premise than a sharply unusual one.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Ralph has a durable contradiction: exhausted provider by day, blocked writer by night, with real shame and tenderness underneath. Maddie, Sarah, Jayden, and Father Phillips each add distinct pressure or support, though Ralph remains the clear center of gravity.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The coal-region setting and custodial world give the script a specific working-class texture, and the screenplay-within-the-screenplay angle adds a nice self-reflexive layer. The execution stays emotionally familiar, with the material leaning on sincerity more than formal boldness.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The 30-day contest deadline and Ralph’s health/work pressure create a usable engine, and the act turns are clear. The middle section is more process-driven than eventful, so the momentum is steady rather than propulsive.

resonant_originality.reasoning: A custodial supervisor secretly writing a script is a clean, immediately legible premise with a strong emotional fit. What keeps it from scoring higher is that the story’s emotional beats and reversals are recognizable rather than surprising.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The coal-region school district, church, diner, and family homestead create a lived-in local ecosystem with economic pressure baked into every scene. The repeated movement between buildings, jobs, and home gives the world story-generating friction.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a consistent, sincere, blue-collar inspirational tone, and it knows exactly what emotional note it wants to land. It doesn’t yet have a sharply ownable tonal blend beyond earnest uplift and working-class melancholy.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are seeds of deeper material in Ralph’s unfinished grief, his marriage history, and the way self-denial becomes identity. The script gestures at that depth, but most of it is surfaced directly rather than held in reserve.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Ralph’s relationships with Maddie, Sarah, Jayden, and Father Phillips all generate usable scenes and distinct emotional functions. Still, this is fundamentally a lead-driven feature rather than an ensemble engine.

lead_characters.name: Ralph Bennett
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 40s, white, working-class, Pennsylvania coal-region resident, father.
lead_characters.hook: A tired but observant second-shift school custodian who has spent years choosing survival over his own creative life. Ralph is funny without trying to be, deeply ashamed of how long he’s been dormant, and quietly electrified by the possibility that he is not too late to become a writer.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a Paul Giamatti or Richard Jenkins-type performance: a contained, emotionally exacting lead who can play fatigue, humor, shame, and late-blooming hope in the same beat. It gives an actor the kind of lived-in transformation role that can reset how the industry sees them.

lead_characters.name: Maddie Bennett
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 17, white, high-school senior, Ralph’s daughter.
lead_characters.hook: Bright, guarded, and more emotionally adult than her age should require, Maddie is the script’s conscience and its pressure valve. She loves her father fiercely, but she refuses to romanticize his sacrifice when it starts costing them both too much.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives a young actor the grounded intelligence and emotional authority of Kaitlyn Dever in Short Term 12 or Beanie Feldstein in Lady Bird. The part lets her play love, frustration, and moral clarity without becoming a stock teen foil.

lead_characters.name: Sarah Martin
lead_characters.demographics: Female, early 30s, English teacher, school employee.
lead_characters.hook: Warm, perceptive, and quietly confident, Sarah is the first adult in Ralph’s orbit who treats his inner life as real. She’s not just a love interest; she’s the person who recognizes the writer before Ralph can admit he exists.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong showcase material in the vein of Emily Blunt in The English Teacher or Laura Linney in You Can Count on Me: intelligent, emotionally legible, and built on subtle chemistry rather than big speeches. It gives an actor a chance to play attraction, encouragement, and restraint with real precision.

lead_characters.name: Jayden
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 17, student, Ralph’s informal writing ally.
lead_characters.hook: Jayden is blunt, calm, and unexpectedly wise for a kid who should be more interested in being cool than being right. He functions as Ralph’s mirror and catalyst, the one person who can call out the quitting before Ralph can hide behind excuses.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of breakout-supporting role that recalls Lucas Hedges in Manchester by the Sea or Jaeden Martell in The Book of Henry: young, sharp, and emotionally catalytic. It gives an actor a scene-stealing mix of intelligence, stillness, and moral force.

lead_characters.name: Father Phillips
lead_characters.hook: Kind but not sentimental, Father Phillips sees Ralph clearly and speaks to him like a man who has watched too many good people disappear into obligation. He’s a steadying presence, but he never lets Ralph off the hook.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets a veteran actor do the understated authority work of Tom Wilkinson in In the Bedroom or Richard Jenkins in The Visitor. It’s a compact but meaningful part with warmth, wit, and moral weight.

lead_characters.name: Marcus Reed
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s-50s, producer, Los Angeles industry professional.
lead_characters.hook: Marcus is the outside-world pressure point who validates Ralph’s work without pretending the path is easy. He’s pragmatic, blunt, and useful, the first person to translate Ralph’s private dream into a professional possibility.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a clean, efficient industry-role part in the lane of Jeffrey Wright in a supporting producer/mentor scene or Paul Sparks as the sharp-eyed professional who changes the temperature of a room. It gives an actor authority without overexposure.

lead_characters.name: Diane Bennett
lead_characters.demographics: Female, deceased in present timeline, Ralph’s wife.
lead_characters.hook: Diane exists primarily through memory and the emotional residue she left behind: practical, loving, and unsentimental about money. She’s the voice of the life Ralph chose, and the one he still has to reconcile with his dream.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of memory role that can land with the ache of Michelle Williams in Manchester by the Sea or Julianne Nicholson in a grief-framed supporting turn. Even in limited screen time, it gives an actor the chance to define the emotional architecture of the lead’s past.

lead_characters.name: Mike
lead_characters.hook: Mike is the younger working-man echo in Ralph’s world: practical, overextended, and trying to do right by his family. He helps show that Ralph’s exhaustion is systemic, not personal weakness.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded supporting role that gives an actor the naturalism of Michael Stuhlbarg in a small but memorable working-class part. It’s a believable, lived-in role that adds texture without demanding a star turn.

casting_characteristics: One key supporting role for a 17-year-old daughter
One 17-year-old student role with substantial dialogue

technical.vfx_details: No visible VFX requirements beyond basic screen inserts and simple title-page graphics.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical water leak/burst pipe sequence, minor prop and set-dressing work, basic classroom and hallway crowd control.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: specialty theatrical with strong streaming afterlife, or direct-to-streaming prestige drama.

budget.note: Contemporary, interior-heavy, and built around a small set of recurring locations with no VFX or stunt load. The main cost pressure is night work across the school and church schedule, not scope creep.

casting.note: Ralph needs an actor who can carry fatigue, humor, and late-blooming creative hunger without playing it sentimental. Maddie and Jayden also need strong young performers who can hold their own in dialogue-heavy scenes.

development.note: The screenplay-within-the-screenplay premise is clear, but the middle section leans process-heavy and the emotional turns are fairly legible. Buyers will likely want to see whether the material can sharpen its dramatic escalation without losing its sincerity.

comp_set.title: The Station Agent
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the small-town, character-first, low-key emotional register and the sense of a damaged adult finding a new way to live inside an unglamorous world.

comp_set.title: The Visitor
comp_set.why_it_comps: Comps on the quiet, late-life reawakening of a man whose identity has been narrowed by routine and grief.

comp_set.title: Paterson
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the poetry-of-work structure, where a blue-collar routine becomes the container for a private artistic life.

comp_set.title: The Pursuit of Happyness
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the inspirational working-class perseverance lane and the father-child emotional engine, even though this script is smaller and more intimate.

comp_set.title: The Holdovers
comp_set.why_it_comps: Comps on the school setting, the emotional friction between adults and a young catalyst, and the melancholy-to-hope tonal arc.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who respond to working-class character dramas about second chances, especially viewers drawn to emotionally sincere stories about fathers, daughters, and creative regret.
audience_target.demographics: 35+, slightly female-skewing but broadly adult; middle-income to upscale specialty audience; strong appeal to viewers who like prestige drama and inspirational indie storytelling.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary, contained, and dialogue-driven with a modest location footprint; the main spend is on school access, night shoots, and a handful of recurring interiors.

types_of_buyers: indie producers seeking awards-adjacent character material
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane of sincere, performance-forward, working-class dramas with a clear emotional hook and manageable production footprint. The school-and-homestead world gives it enough specificity to feel authored without pushing it into expensive territory.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature with a closed emotional arc around Ralph’s late-blooming decision to write; no clear sequel or spinoff vector.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The lead role is a late-blooming showcase.
strengths.what_it_means: This gives buyers a clean actor-first package: a middle-aged working-class lead with humor, shame, tenderness, and a visible internal turn. That is exactly the kind of part that attracts prestige-minded performers and gives a director a performance engine to sell.
strengths.evidence: Ralph’s kitchen scene with the bills and blank notebook, the Jayden confrontation, and the final decision to type his name on the title page.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The working-class setting has real texture.
strengths.what_it_means: The coal-region school district, church, diner, and homestead create a specific world that feels lived-in rather than generic. That specificity helps the film stand out in the prestige-drama lane and gives buyers a clear regional identity to market.
strengths.evidence: The repeated movement between St. Andrew’s Church, the three-building school campus, the family homestead, and the cemetery.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The father-daughter engine is emotionally legible.
strengths.what_it_means: The Ralph-Maddie relationship gives the movie a strong human anchor beyond the writing premise, which broadens the appeal to audiences who want family stakes, not just creative self-discovery. It also gives the film a built-in emotional payoff that can travel in trailers and festival conversation.
strengths.evidence: Maddie’s diner confrontation, her warning that he’s killing himself trying to save her, and her line that she wants him to try.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The screenplay contest gives the story a clean engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The 30-day deadline turns an internal awakening into a concrete commercial device, which helps the film move and gives the marketing team a simple hook. Buyers can immediately understand the stakes without needing a complicated premise.
strengths.evidence: The flyer in Sarah’s classroom, the repeated deadline references, and the final submission/workshop outcome.

strengths.what_it_means: Jayden, Sarah, and Father Phillips each serve a distinct dramatic function, which creates multiple relationship entry points for the audience and for casting. That makes the film feel fuller than a single-protagonist monologue piece and gives supporting actors meaningful scenes.
strengths.evidence: Jayden typing the pages, Sarah reading and validating the script, Father Phillips checking on Ralph’s exhaustion and knee.

whats_special.headline: This is a contained, actor-forward prestige indie with a clean emotional engine: a burned-out school custodian gets one last shot at the writer’s life he abandoned. The low-budget contemporary footprint, specific Pennsylvania world, and father-daughter stakes make it easy to position for specialty buyers who want sincere, performance-driven drama with a clear hook.

items.area: The middle section plays more process than pressure.
items.detail: Once Ralph starts writing, a lot of the act-two material becomes repetition of the same emotional beat: he works, hides, writes, gets encouraged, and keeps going. That’s not a fatal flaw for this lane, but it does mean the script’s momentum is more reflective than propulsive until the health scare and suspension arrive.

items.area: The emotional turns are telegraphed early.
items.detail: Maddie’s concern, Sarah’s encouragement, Jayden’s catalytic bluntness, and Father Phillips’ wisdom all arrive exactly where a reader expects them to. Buyers will likely see the shape of the movie quickly, which helps clarity but limits surprise.

The contest deadline matters, and the suspension raises the temperature, but the story never becomes materially dangerous in a way that would widen the commercial lane. This keeps the film intimate and affordable, but it also caps the sense of urgency for viewers looking for bigger escalation.

items.area: Sarah functions partly as a support beam.
items.detail: She’s appealing and well-positioned, but the script uses her primarily to validate Ralph’s writing and emotional worth. That makes the role useful, but it also means the romantic thread is more functional than fully dramatized.

issues.headline: The script’s main friction is structural rather than conceptual: the premise is clear, but the middle leans on repeated affirmation beats before the suspension and industry call give it a stronger turn. It’s a sincere, castable package, but buyers will notice that the movie’s scale stays deliberately modest throughout.
